home.title: Arabic — Revision
home.intro: Daily-routine Arabic with Arabic script, approximate Latin and Cyrillic reading aids, English and Russian meanings, and practice. The vocabulary uses Modern Standard Arabic; spoken regional varieties differ.
home.source: Source: Revision Booklet 2025-2026, Mrs Hala's group.
home.rtlNote: Arabic is written and read right-to-left (RTL).

learn.title: Learn the words
learn.intro: Arabic script with English and Russian meanings. Latin and Cyrillic reading aids approximate pronunciation; they are not IPA and cannot represent every Arabic sound. Long vowels are doubled in this lesson deck. ʿ marks ع; ʾ marks hamza ء.
learn.legend: EN / RU = meaning · Aa / Аа = approximate reading aid; confirm pronunciation with audio.

flashcards.title: Flashcards
flashcards.intro: See the Arabic, recall the meaning — then flip to check. Pick one block or the whole deck.

exercises.title: Exercises
exercises.intro: The five task types from the booklet. Auto-checked where there is a correct answer; saved as you type where it is open writing.

rearrange.title: A · Re-arrange the sentence
rearrange.instruction: Tap the words in the correct order. Tap a chosen word to put it back.

match.title: B · Match the meaning
match.instruction: Choose the Arabic verb for each English meaning.

create.title: C · Create sentences
create.instruction: Open writing: build your own sentences from the word bank. Your text is saved automatically — there is no auto-check.
create.copyHint: Tap a word to add it to your text.

cloze.title: D · Read and complete
cloze.instruction: Complete the self-introduction. The hint for each blank is shown below it. Your answers are saved.

translate.title: E · Translate
translate.instruction: Read the Arabic, decide the meaning, then reveal the English and Russian.

quiz.title: Quiz
quiz.intro: Choose a block or the full word set. Meanings are contextual glosses of the displayed form; reading-aid questions test recognition, not pronunciation accuracy.
quiz.promptTranslit: Which Arabic item matches this approximate reading aid: “{{value}}”?

mrsHalaPage.title: Mrs Hala's revision — 5 topics
mrsHalaPage.intro: The five topics from your G9 Arabic revision booklet. Master the vocabulary in each, then practise the exercises (rearrange sentences, match meanings, fill in the blanks).
mrsHalaPage.notice: Content directly from your teacher's revision booklet.

introduce.title: 1. Introduce yourself (تقديم نفسك)
phrases: أنا في الصف التاسع (anā fī aṣ-ṣaff at-tāsiʿ) — I am in grade nine; change the grade to suit your situation.
أنا من… (anā min…) — I am from…
أعيش في… (aʿīsh fī…) — I live in…
عمري… سنة (ʿumrī… sana) — I am … years old; Arabic number agreement needs its own rules.
لي إخوة وأخوات (lī ikhwa wa akhawāt) — I have brothers and sisters.

clothes.title: 2. Clothes (الملابس)
vocab: حذاء (ḥidhāʾ) — a shoe; context may imply footwear

Examples: تنورة صفراء قصيرة — a short yellow skirt; بلوزة بيضاء خفيفة — a light white blouse; حذاء أسود — a black shoe; فستان أحمر — a red dress; معطف بني ثقيل — a heavy brown coat; قميص أزرق جديد — a new blue shirt.

colours.title: 3. Colours & adjectives (الألوان والصفات)
vocab: Adjectives: طويل (long), قصير (short), كبير (big), صغير (small), جديد (new), قديم (old), ثقيل (heavy), خفيف (light), جميل (beautiful).
Gender agreement: جديد / جديدة adds ة, but colours such as أحمر / حمراء use a different pattern. Agreement follows the Arabic noun, not the gender of its translation.

routine.title: 4. Daily routine (الروتين اليومي)
times: الساعة الخامسة (5 o'clock), السادسة (6), السابعة (7), الثامنة (8)
صباحًا (ṣabāḥan) — in the morning; a.m. in a clock expression
مساءً (masāʾan) — in the evening; p.m. in a clock expression
Connectors: أولاً (first), ثم (then), حتى (until), بعد ذلك (after that), أخيراً (finally)

extra.title: Question words & connectors
items: ماذا / ما (mādhā / mā) — what
متى (matā) — when
أين (ʾayna) — where
كيف (kayfa) — how
لماذا (limādhā) — why
كم (kam) — how many / how much
إلى — to; في — in/at: prepositions. مع — with/together with: an accompaniment expression traditionally analysed as an adverbial noun, not the same grammatical class as في.

extras.title: Arabic — Extras
extras.intro: Topics beyond the G9 syllabus — numerals, verb patterns, dialects, culture.

numerals.title: Arabic-Indic digits (٠–٩)
numerals.body: Both 0–9 and ٠١٢٣٤٥٦٧٨٩ are used in Arabic-speaking settings, with regional and publication differences. These are positional decimal digits from the Hindu-Arabic numeral tradition. In ٢٠٢٦ the thousands digit is on the left: 2026. The surrounding Arabic script runs right to left; number-word order is a separate issue.

verbForms.title: Ten verb forms (awzān)
verbForms.body: Many Arabic words are built from a consonantal root and a pattern. The familiar forms I–X describe common patterns of triliteral verbs; Arabic also has quadriliteral roots and other patterns. Patterns can suggest meanings, but do not mechanically predict them: كَتَبَ kataba — he wrote; كاتَبَ kātaba — he corresponded with; اسْتَغْفَرَ istaghfara — he sought forgiveness. Form VII is often intransitive or resultative, not the grammatical passive of every verb. Learn the actual verb meaning and conjugation.

dialects.title: Dialects vs MSA
items: Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) — a shared formal variety used in education, publishing and many broadcasts.
Egyptian Arabic — a group of spoken varieties in Egypt; Cairene speech is widely represented in media.
Levantine Arabic — related spoken varieties in Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and Palestine.
Gulf Arabic — related varieties around the Gulf; national borders do not define one uniform dialect.
Maghrebi Arabic — related North African varieties with their own regional histories and multilingual contact.

msa.name: Modern Standard Arabic (MSA)
msa.rule: MSA is a standardised variety used across countries in formal writing and speech. It is related to Classical Arabic but is not identical to all historical or Qur’anic usage. Speakers often shift between standard and regional forms according to setting.
msa.tip: Choose a regional variety for relevant everyday conversations and MSA for the formal contexts you need. No variety is inherently gentler, purer or more refined.

egyptian.name: Egyptian Arabic
egyptian.rule: Egyptian Arabic comprises regional spoken varieties; Cairo speech is prominent in film and other media. Media exposure can help comprehension, but understanding differs between listeners and contexts.
egyptian.tip: Choose a regional variety for relevant everyday conversations and MSA for the formal contexts you need. No variety is inherently gentler, purer or more refined.

levantine.name: Levantine Arabic
levantine.rule: Levantine is a regional grouping, including urban and rural varieties in Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and Palestine. Pronunciation varies: some varieties realise historical q as a glottal stop, while others retain or change it differently.
levantine.tip: Choose a regional variety for relevant everyday conversations and MSA for the formal contexts you need. No variety is inherently gentler, purer or more refined.

gulf.name: Gulf Arabic
gulf.rule: Gulf Arabic (Khaleeji) refers to spoken Arabic varieties used around the Gulf, including in the UAE and Qatar. This regional label does not mean that all speakers use the same pronunciation, vocabulary or grammar; learn the variety relevant to your conversations.
gulf.tip: Choose a regional variety for relevant everyday conversations and MSA for the formal contexts you need. No variety is inherently gentler, purer or more refined.

maghrebi.name: Maghrebi Arabic
maghrebi.rule: Maghrebi Arabic is a broad label for North African Arabic varieties west of Egypt, including Moroccan, Algerian, Tunisian and Libyan varieties. It covers local differences rather than one uniform way of speaking. Familiarity and context affect how much a listener understands.
maghrebi.tip: Choose a regional variety for relevant everyday conversations and MSA for the formal contexts you need. No variety is inherently gentler, purer or more refined.

culture.title: Cultural insights
culture.body: Arabic script can communicate words and also form calligraphic ornament. In a manuscript, tile or vessel, ask what the inscription says, how it is arranged and where the object was made. The Qur’an was transmitted in Arabic, but “Islamic art” is a wider art-historical category that includes secular objects and different regional traditions. Language, religion and nationality are not interchangeable categories.

literature.title: Classics & poetry
items: One Thousand and One Nights — a collection with a frame narrative and a changing textual history.
Mahmoud Darwish — Palestinian poetry of identity, place and displacement.
Naguib Mahfouz — Egyptian novelist; 1988 Nobel laureate.
Nizar Qabbani — Syrian poetry of love, relationships and politics.
Kahlil Gibran — Arabic- and English-language writer; The Prophet was written in English.

nights.name: One Thousand and One Nights
nights.rule: A collection of tales with varied textual histories, framed by Shahrazad telling stories to King Shahriyar. Versions and translations include different stories; there is no single fixed original contents list.

darwish.name: Mahmoud Darwish (1941–2008)
darwish.rule: A Palestinian poet whose work explores displacement, identity, memory, love and place. “Identity Card” is one of his well-known poems. Read a particular poem closely rather than treating all his work as one political message.

mahfouz.name: Naguib Mahfouz (1911–2006)
mahfouz.rule: An Egyptian novelist awarded the 1988 Nobel Prize in Literature. The Cairo Trilogy follows family life and social change across generations. A novel is an artistic representation, not a transparent historical record.

qabbani.name: Nizar Qabbani (1923–1998)
qabbani.rule: A Syrian poet born in Damascus in 1923 who died in London in 1998. His work includes love and political poetry. The publisher Words Without Borders provides a biography and translations for studying particular poems.

gibran.name: Kahlil Gibran (1883–1931)
gibran.rule: A Lebanese-American writer and artist who wrote in Arabic and English. The Prophet (1923) was written in English and uses poetic prose to explore questions such as love, work and freedom. It is not an Arabic original translated into English.
